name: Sara Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I turn French and German product pages into English for online shops: hiking boots, tents, face creams. Last year I left an in-house job at a cosmetics company to go freelance, so I'm still building up clients. Every morning I load the day's batch into an AI tool I've set up with each client's style guide, then spend the day fixing what it gets wrong. I live with my partner Tom, a junior chef, in a small town where the nearest other translation work is an hour's train away.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Better than I feared, worse than I hoped. I've got three regular shops and I'm quicker than most because of my set-up. But the shops pay at the end of the month after next, and I've got about two and a half weeks of rent in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I see every day: the tools are good at the boring ninety percent and bad at the ten percent that sells. I'd write a post about how a tent became 'a house for one sad person' in the raw machine version. Shops love seeing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fine. My whole business is being faster than people who don't use the tools and better than shops that use them alone. If nothing changes, that gap stays. My worry is cash: late payers and a thin cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the three shops and pitch two more, probably the outdoor brands in Lyon I've been eyeing. I'd ask clients for payment in thirty days instead of sixty. I'd try to keep one month's rent in the bank, which I've never had since going freelance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. A bit of cash-flow stress, but that's just freelancing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your pitch to a new shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I show a shop their own product page done three ways, then ask which one they'd buy from. The three are raw machine, a cheap agency, and mine. Usually they pick mine without being told which is which.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever miss the in-house job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The salary, yes, every month. The office, no. I'd go back only if the money got really bad.

say: The tools are good at the **boring ninety percent** and bad at what sells.
I'd post the **tent** that became 'a house for one sad person'.
think: My business is the **speed gap** between me and slower translators.
My worry is **late payers** and a thin cushion.
do: Ask clients for **thirty-day** payment instead of sixty.
Build **one month's rent** in the bank.
S0.quote: I show a shop their own product page done three ways, then ask which one they'd buy from.
fieldNote: She is a **confident early user** and sells the gap between AI and good copy.
Her pressure is **cash flow** from late-paying shops.
Still misses the **in-house salary**, a quiet backup plan.

steps.text: Pitch her three-way product page demo to two outdoor brands
Ask all three shops for thirty-day payment terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here and pretending otherwise is pointless. Product pages are exactly what the card describes, so shops will do more themselves. I'd tell other translators to sell judgement, not words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my per-word work would shrink by half within a year or two. The shops would get their own AI to do the raw version, and only pay me to fix the important pages. I'd survive, but on less, and I've got no cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn myself into a localisation consultant: set up the AI and style guides for each shop, then check the pages that matter. I'd charge per month, not per word. I'd also apply for remote work testing AI translation for language data companies, which pays per task.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but switched on. This is the version where I'd move first and hope I'm right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the shops decide they don't need a consultant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd look at going back in-house, maybe at a bigger online retailer that needs someone to run its translation set-up. I'd hate commuting an hour, but Tom works nights anyway, so we'd barely notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said pretending otherwise is pointless. Who's pretending?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of my old classmates. My friend Léa from university still refuses to touch the tools and charges like it's 2015. Léa is brilliant, but she's going to lose her clients first.

say: AI is here, and **pretending otherwise** is pointless.
Shops will write more of their own **product pages** with AI.
think: My **per-word work** shrinks by half within a year or two.
I'd survive on less, with **no cushion** behind me.
do: Become a **localisation consultant** charging shops per month.
Apply for **AI testing tasks** with language data firms.
Look at **in-house roles** at bigger retailers as a fallback.
feel: **Nervous but switched on**, ready to move first.
S1.quote: My friend Léa from university still refuses to touch the tools and charges like it's 2015. Léa is brilliant, but she's going to lose her clients first.
fieldNote: She expects **real income loss** but already has a pivot ready.
Prices **per month** instead of per word, a smart shift.
Pragmatic judgement of peers, not blame of companies.

steps.text: Sell shops a monthly AI set-up and page review service
Apply for paid AI translation testing with language data firms
Apply in-house at a bigger online retailer if consulting stalls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for everyone, including the people building it. Governments and businesses would need a plan in months, not years. I'd say it calmly, but I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my work is gone by 2028. If the AI is as good as me at judgement, my set-ups and checks are just a step it skips. My job is all screen and thinking, so the robots coming in 2031 changes nothing for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd earn everything I could in the first year and save it. I'd look at a hands-on business with Tom, maybe a small food stall, since cooking has about three more years before robots. I'd use AI to run the stall's ordering and books, so it's just the two of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I like change, but AGI by 2028 is change with no landing spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A food stall is a big leap. Is that realistic with no savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, which is the problem. We'd need a loan or Tom's parents' help. Tom's parents have a bit put by, and they've offered before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your clients?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shops honestly that they don't need me anymore, and offer to set up their AI properly for a final fee. Better to leave on good terms. They might buy from our stall.

say: This is **too fast** for everyone, including the people building it.
Governments and businesses need a **plan in months**.
think: My work is **gone by 2028**; judgement is just a skipped step.
My job is **all screen**, so the robot delay changes nothing.
do: Earn and **save everything** in the first year.
Start a **food stall** with Tom, using AI for orders and books.
Offer shops a **final AI set-up** for a fee.
feel: **Alarmed**: change she likes, but with **no landing spot**.
S2.quote: I like change, but AGI by 2028 is change with no landing spot.
fieldNote: Even an **adaptive** freelancer sees her trade vanish in two years.
Turns to her partner's **hands-on cooking** to use the robot gap.
The plan needs **family money**, which she admits.

steps.text: Save every spare payment from the shops in the first year
Start a small food stall with Tom
Run the stall's ordering and books with AI tools
Ask Tom's parents for help with the stall's start-up costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, but not much, so people should start moving now. I'd tell younger translators to get into something with a skill AI can't do with no body, or with clients who want a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd get three good years from consulting before it fades. That's enough to save and plan properly. I'd still lose the translation work, but I wouldn't be caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the consulting hard and put twenty percent of every payment aside. In year two I'd decide with Tom about the food business and maybe take a short business course. I'd keep my AI skills sharp because they're what earns now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but more excited than scared. Five years is a race I could run. I'd do the consulting hard, save twenty percent of every payment, then jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Twenty percent of every payment. Can you afford that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the consulting goes as I hope, yes. If it doesn't, ten percent, and I'd eat at Tom's restaurant on his staff meal more often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tom say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say yes to the food stall before I finished the sentence. He's wanted his own place since he was nineteen.

say: There's **time, but not much**, so start moving now.
Look for work needing a **body** or a person clients trust.
think: I'd get **three good years** from consulting before it fades.
I'd lose translation but **not be caught out**.
do: Save **twenty percent** of every consulting payment.
Take a short **business course** in year two.
Decide with Tom about the **food business**.
S3.quote: Five years is a race I could run. I'd do the consulting hard, save twenty percent of every payment, then jump.
fieldNote: The five years gives her a **race she can win**: earn, save, jump.
Her partner's **ambition** makes the food plan more real.
Still loses her **trade**, so not calm.

steps.text: Save twenty percent of every consulting payment
Take a short business course in year two
Plan a food business with Tom by year three

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good runway and nobody has an excuse. I'd say it to my clients too, so they think about their own staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have a strong six or seven years, maybe the best of my career, as shops need help setting up. Then it fades. I'd be 37 with savings and a plan, which is more than I've got now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the consulting into a small business, maybe hiring one other translator. I'd build up three months' savings by year two. By year five I'd have a decision made with Tom about the food business or something else hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good. A bit wary, because ten years has a way of becoming five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean, ten years becomes five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I went freelance, I thought I'd have two years to build up. Things move faster than plans. It took four months before my old company replaced me with an agency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you hire someone like Léa?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If she'd learn the tools, yes, in a heartbeat. She's better with French than me. That's the honest truth.

I'd tell clients to think about **their own staff**.
think: I'd have a strong **six or seven years** helping shops set up.
At **37** I'd have savings and a plan.
do: Grow consulting into a **small business** and hire a translator.
Build **three months' savings** by year two.
Decide on a **hands-on business** with Tom by year five.
feel: **Mostly good**, wary that ten years becomes five.
S4.quote: When I went freelance, I thought I'd have two years to build up. Things move faster than plans.
fieldNote: The decade could be her **best earning stretch** before the fade.
Her own **freelance story** makes her distrust long timelines.

steps.text: Hire a second translator for the AI consulting business
Build three months' savings by the end of year two

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no landing spot, even for someone who loves the tools. What would help is cheap loans for small hands-on businesses, so people like Tom and me could start something without parents' money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what translators are actually good at. A translator's real skill isn't words. It's knowing what a customer in Lyon will think when they read a sentence. I don't know if AI ever really gets that.

headlineQuote: A translator's real skill isn't words. It's knowing what a customer in Lyon will think when they read a sentence.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old** French and German product page translator, freelance for a year, living with chef Tom.
She uses AI **every day** and sells the gap between machine output and copy that sells.
Cash flow is tight: **late-paying shops** and about two and a half weeks saved.
Pragmatic, she **moves first** and doesn't blame anyone in particular.
In fast scenarios she turns to a **food business** with Tom; slower ones become an earning runway.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no landing spot even for heavy AI users.
